analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent the lowered tax rates on capital gains and stock dividends for individuals.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a vote, after 22 of 40 Senate Republicans cosponsored it.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2003 Bush tax cuts lowered the tax rate on investment income—profits from selling stocks and other assets, and dividends paid to shareholders—but included an expiration date so those rates would end after 2010 unless Congress renewed them. This bill would have deleted that expiration date, locking in the lower rates permanently. It never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died at the end of the 111th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with large investment income gain the most, since capital gains and dividends are concentrated among high earners; investment funds and asset managers also gain because permanent low rates make taxable investment funds more attractive and avoid a scheduled rate increase that fund investors and their clients would have paid. Supporters also argued permanent rates give investors planning certainty and keep the after-tax return on investment higher.

how_it_helps.text: Deletes the expiration date in the 2003 tax law, so the reduced individual tax rates on capital gains and dividends do not end on schedule [S2] [S3].
Because the 2003 rates were set to terminate after 2010, making them permanent prevents a scheduled increase in the tax rate on investment income [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury bears the cost of the permanently lower rates, and the revenue gap must be made up by other taxpayers, through borrowing, or through spending cuts. The benefits of lower capital-gains and dividend rates are concentrated among households that own significant investments, so the direct tax savings go overwhelmingly to high earners.

drawbacks.text: Permanently lower rates on capital gains and dividends reduce federal revenue, and the largest savings go to households with the most investment income [S2] [S3].

Supporters of letting the rates expire as scheduled argued the reductions were designed to be temporary and that making them permanent added to long-term deficits; the bill contained no offset to cover the lost revenue [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers permanent certainty and lower rates to investors, which supporters value for encouraging investment, but it does so with no way to pay for the lost revenue, and the direct benefits are concentrated among the households that hold the most capital gains and dividends. The revenue cost falls on everyone who relies on the federal budget, so the tradeoff favors concentrated interests over broad public finance.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Crapo introduced the bill on March 11, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance [S1] [S5].
Twenty-two of the Senate's 40 Republicans cosponsored the bill [S4].
The action history shows no further steps after the referral—no committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the lower investment-income rates were not made permanent at that time, preserving federal revenue that would have been forgone—mainly for the benefit of households with the largest investment income. The George W. Bush administration-era rates did continue past 2010 through later, separate legislation, so the practical relief was temporary rather than permanent from this bill's death alone.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal revenue; the scheduled rate increase took effect on time

for.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the reduced capital gains and dividend rates permanent and led its introduction.

for.name: 22 of 40 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Chair Max Baucus)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral—no markup, no vote, and it never reached the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was entirely Republican: Senator Crapo sponsored it and all 22 cosponsors were Senate Republicans; no Democrats signed on.

industries.note: Permanent low rates on capital gains and dividends would raise the after-tax returns of households and funds that live on investment income, a group concentrated at the top of the income distribution. The cost is forgone federal revenue that other taxpayers must cover.

Permanent dividend and capital-gains preferences make taxable fund and brokerage accounts more attractive relative to other vehicles, supporting flows into these products. The benefit to the industry comes from the same forgone revenue that ordinary taxpayers absorb.
